definition: In theoretical linguistics and computational linguistics, probabilistic context free grammars (PCFGs) extend context-free grammars, similar to how hidden Markov models extend regular grammars.
details: Each production is assigned a probability. The probability of a derivation (parse) is the product of the probabilities of the productions used in that derivation. These probabilities can be viewed as parameters of the model, and for large problems it is convenient to learn these parameters via machine learning. A probabilistic grammar's validity is constrained by context of its training dataset. PCFGs originated from grammar theory and have applications ranging from natural language processing to the study of RNA structure and the design of programming languages. Designing efficient PCFGs has to weigh factors of scalability and generality. Issues such as grammar ambiguity must be resolved. The grammar design affects results accuracy. Grammar parsing algorithms have various time and memory requirements.

explainer.lead: A probabilistic context-free grammar extends a context-free grammar by assigning a probability to each production. It matters because it lets parsers rank competing parses instead of treating all as equally valid.

tiers.eli5: It's a set of sentence-building rules where each rule has a likelihood, so some ways of building a sentence are judged more probable than others.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use PCFGs to score parses, typically taking the product of production probabilities along a derivation and learning the parameters from data. A pitfall is that a grammar's validity is constrained by the context of its training dataset, so it generalises poorly beyond it.
tiers.paperLevel: Each production is assigned a probability; the probability of a derivation (parse) is the product of the probabilities of the productions used in it. These probabilities are model parameters, conveniently learned via machine learning for large problems, and the grammar's validity is constrained by its training data context.

explainer.example: For a sentence with two possible parses, the grammar ranks them by multiplying the probabilities of the productions in each derivation and choosing the higher product.
